title: AWS access key leaked in a public GitHub repository at a B2B software company
summary: On a Friday night AWS warns that one of the company's access keys is sitting in a public GitHub repository. The key runs production deploys, a large customer goes live on Monday, and by morning the bill shows servers nobody started and the logs cannot say for certain whether customer files were copied. The exercise tests who may break production to contain an incident, how the group decides on incomplete evidence, and when customers are told.

setting.company_profile: A 40-person B2B software company that runs its product on AWS, keeps code on GitHub, works in Slack and Google Workspace, and holds customer records in a database and S3 file storage. It is partway through its annual security audit and sells to enterprise customers whose contracts set deadlines for breach notice.
setting.day_and_time: Friday, 9:26 p.m., the weekend before a large customer's Monday go-live
setting.initial_signal: An automated email from AWS reaches the shared ops mailbox and is copied into the Slack #ops channel: an access key belonging to the company has been found in a public GitHub repository and should be treated as compromised. The on-call engineer reads it on a phone.

roles.name: Incident Commander
roles.responsibilities: Runs the response from the moment the AWS email is read, decides when the deploy key is switched off despite Monday's go-live, and keeps one list of open decisions and their owners.

roles.name: Technical Lead
roles.responsibilities: Replaces the leaked key, removes whatever was created with it in AWS, and reports plainly what CloudTrail and the S3 logs can and cannot prove.

roles.name: Communications Lead
roles.responsibilities: Writes the reply to the go-live customer's security team and any wider customer notice, and makes sure nobody answers customers on their own in Slack or email.

roles.name: Legal and Compliance Lead
roles.responsibilities: Reads the notice clauses in customer contracts, tracks each deadline, brings in outside counsel and decides what the auditor is given.

roles.name: Executive Sponsor
roles.responsibilities: Approves the decisions that cost money or revenue: freezing deploys, delaying the go-live, paying the AWS charges and notifying customers before the facts are complete.

roles.name: Scribe
roles.responsibilities: Keeps the timeline in the incident Slack channel: every finding, decision, owner and time, starting with the AWS email at 9:26 p.m.

objectives: Decide who may switch off a production credential on a Friday night when the CTO cannot be reached.
Confirm the team can list everything a leaked AWS key did: servers started, users created and files read.
Agree what evidence is enough to treat customer data as accessed when logging is incomplete, and who makes that call.
Name who tracks the notice deadlines in customer contracts and who approves the first written statement to a customer.
Decide what must be true before deploys resume and the incident is closed.

injects.title: AWS reports a company access key in a public repository
injects.narrative: Friday, 9:26 p.m. An automated email from AWS reaches the shared ops mailbox and is copied into the Slack #ops channel. It says an access key belonging to the company has been found in a public GitHub repository and should be treated as compromised. An access key is a password that software, rather than a person, uses to sign in to AWS. The on-call engineer reads it on a phone. The repository is a sample project that one of the company's engineers published earlier this evening for a customer workshop on Monday. Nothing looks broken and no customer has complained. The CTO, who would normally make the call, is at a family event and not answering. The on-call engineer has never declared an incident and is not sure the plan allows it.
questions: Who can declare an incident on a Friday night when the CTO cannot be reached, and where is that written down?
Is a leaked key with no visible damage worth calling people in tonight, and who makes that call?
Where does the group run the response, and who must be told in the first 15 minutes?
expected_actions: The on-call engineer declares an incident, acts as Incident Commander until relieved, and phones the backup decision maker named in the plan.
Open a dedicated Slack channel for the response and post every finding and decision there with its time.
Look the key up in the AWS IAM console to see which user it belongs to and what it is allowed to do.

injects.title: The leaked key runs production deploys
injects.narrative: The on-call engineer looks the key up in IAM, the part of AWS that manages users and keys. It belongs to the deploy pipeline, the automated process in GitHub Actions that ships new code to production. It has administrator permissions, far more than deploys need, and has not been changed in two years. The nightly job that writes customer export files to S3, the AWS file storage, uses the same key. Switching it off now stops all deploys and tonight's 1:00 a.m. exports until a replacement is made and tested, perhaps three hours of work. Monday's go-live depends on a fix that has not been deployed yet. The engineer who published the repository is mortified and offers to delete it, rewrite its history so the key disappears, and replace the key quietly on Monday.
questions: Who decides to switch the key off tonight, knowing deploys and the 1:00 a.m. export job stop until a replacement is tested?
Does deleting the repository make the key safe again, and who tells the engineer what to do and what to leave alone?
Who tells the account manager for Monday's go-live that deploys are frozen, and when?
expected_actions: Make the leaked key inactive in the AWS IAM console tonight, then create a replacement limited to what deploys need and store it in GitHub Actions secrets.
Ask the engineer to switch the repository to private without deleting it or rewriting its history, so the record of what was public and when is kept.
Message the account manager for Monday's go-live tonight: deploys are frozen, and the next update comes at a stated time.

injects.title: Saturday morning: servers nobody started and a new administrator
injects.narrative: Saturday, 7:15 a.m. The billing alarm posts in Slack: month-to-date AWS spend has more than doubled overnight. The billing page shows 58 large GPU servers running in three regions the company has never used, costing about $410 an hour. CloudTrail, the AWS log of who did what in the account, shows the leaked key started them at 9:14 p.m. on Friday, minutes after the repository went public and before the AWS email had even arrived. It also shows the key creating a new user with administrator rights and an access key of its own. Whatever was done to the leaked key last night, that user is still active. One engineer wants everything deleted now to stop the charges. Another says the servers and the user are evidence and must not be touched.
questions: Who decides between deleting the servers to stop the charges and keeping them as evidence, and is there a way to do both?
How does the group confirm it has found everything the leaked key created, and who signs off that the AWS account is clean?
Who contacts AWS Support about the charges, and who can approve paying them if AWS says no?
expected_actions: Disable the unknown user and its access key in IAM first, then stop the unfamiliar servers in the EC2 console without deleting them, and note their IDs, regions and start times.
Download the CloudTrail event history for the leaked key and the new user, and save it where only the Incident Commander and Technical Lead can change it.
Open an AWS Support case reporting the compromised key, ask what AWS needs before it will consider adjusting the bill, and name one person to answer it.

injects.title: Were customer files read? The logs do not settle it
injects.narrative: By 9:30 a.m. the question has moved from cost to data. The S3 bucket that holds customer export files keeps an access log. It shows 4,300 files read with the leaked key between 9:16 p.m. and 9:48 p.m. on Friday, covering exports for 31 customers. A weekly backup job also reads that bucket on Friday nights with the same key, and the engineer who wrote it is sure that is all this is. But the job is scheduled for 11:30 p.m., well after these reads ended. For the customer database and the 14 other buckets, detailed logging was never switched on, so there is no record either way. The CEO joins the call and asks for a yes or no: was customer data taken?
questions: With an engineer's certainty on one side and the log on the other, does the group treat the 31 customers' files as accessed, and who decides?
What does the Incident Commander tell the CEO right now, in one sentence, and what can the group not yet say?
For the database and the 14 buckets with no logging, what does the group assume, and who writes that assumption down?
expected_actions: Record a working assumption that a stranger read the export files of the 31 customers, and name who can overturn it and on what evidence.
The Technical Lead checks the backup job's run history against the network addresses in the S3 access log and reports back at a set time.
List the 31 customers by name, and check CloudTrail for any copies or exports of the customer database made by the leaked key or the new user.

injects.title: The go-live customer already knows
injects.narrative: Saturday, 11:10 a.m. The security team at the customer going live on Monday emails the account manager. A monitoring service they use flagged a public repository containing the company's name and what looked like a cloud key. They want three answers in writing by 9:00 a.m. Monday: was the key real, was their data touched, and what has been done. Without them, the go-live is postponed. Their contract requires notice within 48 hours of the company becoming aware of a suspected security incident affecting their data, and their exports are among the 31. Most of the other 30 customers have similar clauses. The account manager has drafted a reply saying the exposure was brief and no customer was affected, and wants to send it now, before anyone else has read it.
questions: Does a suspected, unproven read of export files already trigger the 48-hour clause, and who decides that?
Who approves the reply to this customer, and can it say that no customer was affected?
Do the other 30 customers hear from the company before this customer's Monday deadline or after it, and who owns that list?
expected_actions: Hold the account manager's draft; the Communications Lead and the Legal and Compliance Lead rewrite it to say what is confirmed, what is still being checked and when the next update will come.
Copy the notice clause from each of the 31 customer contracts in Google Drive into one sheet with deadline, security contact and owner.
Call outside counsel today, before any written statement leaves the company, and agree who signs customer notices.

injects.title: Go-live, clean-up and closing the incident
injects.narrative: Sunday, 4:00 p.m. The checks are back. The backup job did not make those reads: all 4,300 came from two network addresses nobody at the company can identify. A replacement deploy key works in a test. Nobody can say for sure whether the old key was also copied to laptops, the staging environment or older repositories. AWS Support will consider adjusting the bill once the company confirms in writing that the account is secured. The go-live fix is still not deployed, and the customer's 9:00 a.m. deadline is 17 hours away. Engineering wants to deploy tonight and close the incident. The operations manager who coordinates the annual audit points out that it covers this weekend: the auditor will ask for the incident record, the timeline and proof that the plan was followed.
questions: Who decides whether Monday's go-live goes ahead, and what must be true about the AWS account before production deploys resume?
Now that a stranger's reads are confirmed, who sends notice to the 31 customers, and which contract has the earliest deadline?
Who declares the incident closed, against what checklist, and what record is handed to the auditor?
expected_actions: Search GitHub repositories, GitHub Actions secrets, laptops and the staging environment for the old key and any other long-lived AWS keys, and replace what is found before deploys resume.
Send written notice to the security contacts of all 31 customers, approved by counsel and the Executive Sponsor, starting with the go-live customer.
Reply to AWS Support listing the clean-up steps completed, and save the Slack channel export, timeline and decision log where the auditor can be given them.

wrap_up_questions: Which decisions did the plan answer outright, and at which points did the group have to improvise?
What was missing on Friday night: a backup for the CTO, a list of where long-lived AWS keys are used, logging on customer data, or a sheet of customer notice clauses?
What will change in the plan and in the AWS and GitHub setup because of this exercise, and by what date?
Who owns each change, and who will show the auditor that it was made?
